trace.content: {"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Myasthenia Gravis", "confidence": 0.98}, {"diagnosis": "Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome", "confidence": 0.25}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy", "confidence": 0.15}, {"diagnosis": "Mitochondrial Myopathy (e.g., Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia)", "confidence": 0.32}, {"diagnosis": "Seronegative Myasthenia Gravis", "confidence": 0.45}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.912, "reasoning": "The clinical triad—fatigable diplopia, ptosis worsening with sustained upward gaze, proximal limb weakness improving with rest—strongly supports myasthenia gravis (MG). The presence of elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies (AChR-Ab) is highly specific (>99%) for generalized MG in this age and sex context. Repetitive nerve stimulation showing decremental response on EMG further confirms postsynaptic neuromuscular junction dysfunction. Normal chest CT rules out thymoma but does not exclude non-thymomatous MG (which constitutes ~85% of AChR-Ab+ cases). Seronegative MG is less likely here given positive AChR-Ab, but included at moderate confidence (0.45) to acknowledge rare false-negative assay interpretations or borderline titers—though the test result explicitly states 'Present (elevated)'. Lambert-Eaton is unlikely due to absence of autonomic symptoms, absent areflexia (reflexes are normal), and lack of presynaptic antibody markers (e.g., VGCC-Ab not reported); its typical presentation includes improvement with exercise—not fatigue—and no ocular predominance. CIDP is implausible: it causes symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy with areflexia, sensory deficits, and CSF/nerve conduction abnormalities—not fatigable ocular or proximal myopathic weakness. Mitochondrial myopathy may cause ptosis and ophthalmoparesis, but it is typically progressive without diurnal fluctuation or rest improvement, lacks AChR-Ab, and usually shows ragged-red fibers or mtDNA mutations—none supported here. Thus, classic AChR-Ab-positive generalized MG is overwhelmingly the most probable diagnosis."}
